Foreword 
For most of my career, the software we secured did what it was told. 
It followed the rules we wrote, executed the steps we defined, and 
waited for a person to make the consequential decisions. That single 
assumption silently shaped nearly every control we built. This year, it 
stopped being true.
The chapters ahead are about agentic AI, the systems that reason, 
plan, and act on their own. An agent can now open a ticket, query a 
database, call an API, and hand work off to another agent, making 
dozens of decisions in a single workflow with no human in the loop. 
That is not simply a faster version of the software we already knew. It 
is a new kind of actor operating inside our environments at machine 
speed, and it changes the questions security teams have to ask.

Nonhuman Identity as a First-Class Consideration
Every agent needs its own identity with temporary, scoped credentials with scoped access, rather than sharing a credential 
that allows broad access. This allows organizations to extend Zero Trust principles to AI agents. Every request must 
be authenticated and authorized independently, and every action needs a traceable authorization chain. Meeting this 
standard requires:
•  Ephemeral credentials—Agents receive temporary credentials with scoped access rather than persistent access. 
Identity life cycle management must operate at machine speed.
•  Independent authorization—Authorization is enforced independently of the model and scoped to least privilege.
•  Context-aware permissions—An agent acts on behalf of a user, so its permissions should be scoped to only the

For example, an agent handling a routine data lookup for an authorized user operates with read-only access to a
